E-Commerce Promises and Error Handling Lab


This Project

This project was created to help me practice and understand using Promises, API calls, and error handling in TypeScript.

The project simulates an e-commerce dashboard that gets information about products, reviews, and sales. Since API calls can fail, I also practiced using .catch() and .finally() to handle errors.

This lab was confusing for me at first because asynchronous code does not always run in the order I expected.

What I Practiced

In this project, I practiced:

Promises
.then()
.catch()
.finally()
API simulation
Custom error classes
Error handling
Retry functions
Critical Thinking Questions

1. Why is it important to handle errors for each API call?

It is important because different API calls can fail for different reasons. If one API fails, I wanted to know which request caused the problem. This made it easier to find and fix the error.

At first, I thought one error message at the end would be enough, but I started to understand that knowing exactly which API failed is more helpful.

2. How do custom error classes improve debugging?

Custom error classes make errors easier to understand.

A NetworkError tells me that the problem may be related to the network or connection.

A DataError tells me that there may be a problem with the information that came back from the API.

I am still getting used to custom error classes, but I understand that they help identify what type of problem happened.

3. When is a retry mechanism useful?

A retry mechanism can be useful when an API fails because of a temporary problem, such as a slow network connection.

Instead of stopping the program right away, the program can wait and try the request again.

The retry part was one of the more confusing parts for me because it uses more advanced logic, but I understand the basic idea.

Reflection

I found Promises and asynchronous programming more difficult than some of the JavaScript concepts I learned earlier.

At first, I was confused by .then(), .catch(), and .finally() because the code does not always feel like it runs straight from top to bottom.

Breaking the Promise chain into smaller steps helped me understand it a little better. I started to see that .then() is used when something works, .catch() is used when something goes wrong, and .finally() runs at the end.

I also learned that API calls can fail, so error handling is important.

I still need more practice with Promises, custom errors, and retry functions, but this lab helped me understand the basic idea of asynchronous programming a little better.
